Resources, Land, and Exit Terms

Who has the title to the land? This is very important! Whoever holds the title has a great deal of power over the community. If the deed is in the founder's name, for instance, then they're essentially a landlord with a philosophy. If three out of twelve members own everything, then there are really two classes of members, despite what the group's literature may say about everyone being equal.

What legal form will hold the land: a cooperative, trust, association, company, or whatever fits your jurisdiction? Decide that before the land is bought. Then you need to decide voting rights and access/use rights for shared resources, and contribution accounting if you use it. Work out inheritance and outside debt, how improvements get handled, and what happens when somebody leaves. That’s a lot of deciding, I realize.

Visibility is important even in a money-free community. There are always scarce things and bottlenecks. It is important that people be able to know what the community owns or holds in common, what is set aside, what it owes to outsiders. Who has authority over distribution of major resources? Where are the conflicts of interest? Large transfers (land, equipment, stores or outside cash) can't depend on one person's memory or permission. It is also important to specify what rights people have to resources when they leave the community. Whether or not the community uses money, it still needs to be able to provide people with resources when they leave, in whatever form makes sense (cash if it uses money, but also tools, transportation, temporary housing, stored goods or the right to keep using something). Otherwise the "right" to leave is just something on paper that can only be exercised if the community has spare money. That's not much of a right.

Good people leave for good reasons, like a dying parent, love, work, health, exhaustion, or just a simple change of mind. Leaving should not require someone to leave everything they’ve put in, as that’s effectively coercing someone to stay. You should write down the exit terms while no one is leaving yet, and it’s still just a theoretical discussion. Think of it as a pre-nup while you’re planning the wedding. It’s not that romantic, but it’s protective, and a lot easier than doing it when people are furious.

For the full sequence, see Diana Leafe Christian’s Creating a Life Together: the vision comes before the members, the members before you pool the major resources, and the land comes last. (It's in the reading list at the end, too.)
l02:
Do visitors, volunteers, workers, renters and interns at a commune need some rights even if they're not fully "in" the commune politically? (Yes, even the interns!) When decisions really affect their pay or access to shared resources, they need clear terms and a way to be heard, and those decisions have to be open to review. Also when decisions really affect their schedule, safety, housing, records or discipline. Equality isn't just for members, or else there's a risk of recreating a servant class that moves from commune to commune.

When Somebody Has to Go

A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. Yes, really. If someone is a serious or general danger, keeps violating essential boundaries, or is just impossible to live with, ejecting them can be the right call. If restorative work with them can work in a reasonable amount of time, that’s cool! But if they are a danger to the community, the community doesn’t have to turn into their treatment program.

On the other hand, the power to remove people is also one of the easiest to abuse. So work out the process before it's about anyone in particular. What conduct might constitute cause for immediate action to protect people? Who will decide whether to place temporary restrictions on someone? Who will preserve the evidence? Who will recuse themselves? How can the person reply, and what review or appeal is possible without endangering others? What will be done to protect their housing, records, family contact, and access to common resources or outside funds (if any) during separation? When will outside help be sought? (More on that next.)
